lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Senior Advocate (Mahmudul Islam and Zakir Ahmed, Advocates with him) instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant. 
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Mohammad Eunus and Brothers (Pvt) Ltd ----- Appellant. 
Vs. 
University of Chittagong through the Registrar ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J.: By a judgment and order dated the 28th November 1989 the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1988 made the Arbitrator's award dated the 20th May 1989 a Rule of the Court. In First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 261 of 1990 a Division Bench of the High Court Division by judgment and order dated the 13th January 1991 set aside the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge and the impugned award. The awardee has preferred this appeal by leave there from. 

 2. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submission as to whether the High Court Division erred in holding that the Arbitrator misconducted himself in considering the proceedings of the 87th meeting of the Planning and Development Committee (P & D Committee, in short) of the University of Chittagong as a part of the contract, whether it was also wrong in holding that the Arbitrator's finding on the actual quantity of earth cut by the appellant was without any basis, whether the award was indefinite and vague, whether even on that assumption the award could be remitted under section 16 of the Arbitration Act to the learned Subordinate Judge and as to whether the High Court Division failed to notice that the contract itself provided for payment of interest denied to the appellant by the High Court Division. 

 15. The work was stopped during the joint measurement with the concurrence of both sides. The contractor-appellant addressed a letter to the Vice-Chancellor of the University on 22.6.87 drawing his attention to various matters including correction of the contract, design, drawing and other matters. No specific answer was given to this letter. The contractor-appellant was directed to resume the work within 7 days by letter dated 26.6.87. The contractor-appellant replied to the letter and sought redress of his grievances made out in the letter dated 22.6.87. After a lapse of nearly 10 months the respondent-University by letter dated 5.4.88 asked the appellant to resume the work within 15 days. On 10.4.88 the appellant by a letter replied to the notice and requested the University authorities to settle the dispute with regard to earthwork. On 5.4.88 the University authorities cancelled the contract and informed the contractor-appellant of the same. The contractor-appellant demanded a sum of Tk. 26,10,000.00 from the respondent-University and asked for arbitration as per contract. The Vice- Chancellor was the designated Arbitrator. As the Vice-Chancellor failed to arbitrate in the matter the contractor-appellant obtained the appointment of Engineer Alhaj Md. Aflatoon, then the Chief Establishment Officer (East), Bangladesh Railway, Chittagong as the sole Arbitrator on an application before the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1988 by an order dated 29.9.88. 

 18. The contractor-appellant filed the award in Court for making it a Rule of the Court under section 8 of the Arbitration Act in Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1988 and the respondent-University apart from filing a written objection thereto also filed an application under sections 33/30 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the award. 

 20. The respondent-University appealed and the main grounds on which the High Court Division allowed the appeal was that the Arbitrator misconducted himself by treating the proceedings of the 87th meeting of the P&D Committee of the University as a part of the contract itself because the contract did not mention any specific quantity of earth to be cut on account of item No. 1 of the work schedule. The quantity of earth to be cut was not an ascertained or definite figure. The whole work of earth cutting on account of item No. 1 was to be done for a lumpsum amount of Tk. 34 lakh, whatever be the quantity of earth. The High Court Division further held that the Arbitrator without any material on record and on an imaginary, hypothetical and unfounded basis determined the quantum of earth already cut by the contractor-appellant It further held that the award was not for any ascertained and definite amount and therefore the same was otherwise invalid being vague and indefinite. In respect of interest the High Court Division held that it is now well-settled that an Arbitrator, not being a Court, cannot award any interest 

 22. It is true, he submits, that the quantum of earthwork has not been mentioned either in the tender notice or in the schedule or in the agreement, but the agreement itself does not contain any schedule of work. The schedule of work has been annexed to the work order. As such, he submits, the agreement cannot be understood at all if it is not read with the work order. The relevant portion of the work order dated 16.1.87 has already been quoted in full and Mr. Ahmed submits that there is a clear reference therein that the work in question has been entrusted to the appellant not only with reference to the appellant's tender dated 30.8.86 but also with reference to subsequent discussions in the P & D Committee in its 84th and 87th meeting held on 11.9.86 and 11.1.87 respectively. Mr. Ahmed then draws our attention to the proceedings of the 87th meeting which have already been quoted in full and submits that there is a clear decision after detailed discussion that the contract was for a lumpsum amount of Tk. 34 lakh for cutting a specific quantity of 32 lakh cubic feet of earth. Even if this understanding or agreement was not incorporated in either the Agreement itself or in the Schedule of work annexed to the work order, yet the very reference to the proceedings of the 87th meeting in the work order makes the proceedings a part of the contract itself. The High Court Division, therefore, was in error in finding that the Arbitrator misconducted himself in treating the proceedings of the 87th meeting as a part of the contract itself. 

 23. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the respondent-University, submits, on the other hand, that the P&D Committee of the University .was only a recommendatory body and it had no authority to enter into a contract with the appellant: Its deliberations are in the nature of negotiations. The University may have calculated initially through its Engineering Consultants that only 42,60,000 cubic feet of earthwork is involved in the project and its P&D Committee may have subsequently calculated that only 32 lakh cubic feet earth work is involved in the project, but the appellant as a prudent contractor was required to visit the site, make his own measurement, see the drawings and calculate whether he could do the work within the price quoted and negotiated. If it is his case that the University authorities misled him by projecting misleading figures of quantity of earthwork his remedy lies in a suit for damages and the University may take such defences in such a suit as it may be advised. But when the appellant asked for arbitration on a contract the contract itself must be a contract for cutting 32 lakh cubic feet of earth for a lumpsum amount of Tk. 34 lakh, which it is not. Neither in the tender document, nor in the agreement dated 16.1.87 nor in the Schedule of work contained in the work order dated 16.1.87, nor in the running bills in which approval for payment was made, has it been acknowledged or noted that the contract was for a lumpsum amount for cutting a specific quantity of earth. The appellant clearly knew that the contract was for a lumpsum amount for cutting an indefinite quantity of earth and that is why he sought for rectification of the contract by his letter dated 22.6.87. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed further submits that Article l(a) of the Tender Document does not make the covering letter dated 16.1.87, the work order, as a part of the contract. 

 24. It is clear, and the contractor-appellant admits, that there was no quantification of earth either in the Tender Document or in the Agreement dated 26.1.87 or in the Schedule of work annexed to the work order dated 16.1.87. Nevertheless it is also clear that the Engineering Consultants of the University prior to the floating of the tender estimated 42,60,000 cubic feet of earthwork to be involved in the project. Although the contractor-appellant was not supposed to know this figure as it was never communicated officially to him, it is clear from the proceedings of the 87th meeting of the P & D Committee that this figure was disclosed to him and it was further represented to him that the earthwork may not be of that magnitude after all. It will be for a much reduced quantity of 32 lakh cubic feet we find that the appellant proportionately reduced the tender amount keeping in view the reduction in the quantity of earthwork. In the proceedings of the 87th meeting it is clearly stated that the appellant was to be paid Tk. 34 lakh for cutting 32 lakh cubic feet of earth. If the matter stayed there perhaps it could be said that the said proceedings were a part of the negotiating process initiated by a recommendatory body and were not a part of the contract itself, but in issuing the work order dated 16.1.87 the appellant was clearly referred to the subsequent discussions in the P&D Committee in its 87th meeting. The proceedings of a recommendatory body were thus given a formal recognition by the respondent itself. The work order became very much an instrument necessary for the understanding of the contract. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that the operative words of the work order merely referred to the "negotiated rate" at the said meeting but not to the quantity as it was impossible to quantify the earthwork which could only remain a guess work. Reading the work order as a whole we find this restricted reading to be impossible. The discussions that were held in the 87th meeting were not only in respect of reduced rate but also in respect of reduced quantity of earthwork. This is not a case of the appellant being misled by the representations of the University leading to a suit for damages, but a clear case of interpretation of contract with reference to admitted contemporaneous documents. The quantification of earthwork does not find place in any of the contract documents, no doubt, but by reference to the 87th meeting of the P&D Committee, both parties give an interpretation to item No. 1 of the Schedule of work. Though not a part of the contract itself it is a contemporaneous document accepted by both sides throwing light on the interpretation of item No. 1 of the Schedule of work. We do not think that the Arbitrator misconducted himself in this regard and therefore the relevant finding of the High Court Division is erroneous and not sustainable. 

 27. It is true that neither the contractor nor the University maintained any documents or papers showing the actual quantity of earth already cut by the contractor but it is precisely for this reason that the Arbitrator was required to arrive at a figure after considering the evidence on record. We find that it is the case of both sides that no earth has yet been cut from the northern side of Kata Pahar and the contractor has cut earth from the southern side only. In arriving at the quantity of earth cut from the southern side the Arbitrator has taken into consideration the speed with which the work was accomplished as per written objection of the respondent itself, as per records maintained by the respondent, as per approximate calculations made in the running bills and the calculations of the respondent itself as to the remaining earth in the northern and southern sides of the hill. It is not true, as contended by Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, that in the running bills the approximate calculation was made in terms of the lumpsum amount only and not in terms of the total quantity of earthwork. The relevant observations of the respondent authority in the running bills are: "work done approximately 22%," "work done approximately 33%," "work done approximately 34%". There is no misreading of the running bills at all. The Arbitrator has also taken into consideration the rate of progress of work as maintained by the respondent, the expected progress of work and the convention of deducting 10% from the running bills and coming as it does from an Engineer Arbitrator, it cannot be said that he was wide off the mark. In the absence of documents the Arbitrator's work was indeed a difficult one and unless it can be shown that his conclusions were based totally on no evidence and on pure guesswork, his labour cannot be allowed to be wasted on a critical analysis of his method of reasoning. It was perfectly possible for another Arbitrator to take a different view of the quantum of earth already cut but as long as the Arbitrator's finding is based on the evidence he received and on empirical deductions not challenged on any engineering principle, his finding cannot be disturbed as without any basis. The High Court Division, therefore, wrongly rejected the Arbitrator's findings in this regard. 

 28. With regard to the vagueness of the award Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that in respect of earthwork the Arbitrator awarded a sum of Tk. 34 lakh minus the sums which he has already drawn against the first, second and third running bills and the award cannot be held to be indefinite and vague on that account because the amount can easily be ascertained and in any case if it is unascertainable the award could be remitted under section 16 of the Arbitration Act to the learned Subordinate Judge. 

 Latifur Rahman J : Agreeing with the judgment of my learned brother Mustafa Kamal J, I want to add few words in support of his judgment, as a question has squarely come up as to whether in interpreting the formal contract, the contemporaneous documents could be considered as a part of the formal contract as it unmistakably reveals the true intention of the parties in view of the peculiar circumstances of the case. 

 38. The facts of the case have been so elaborately described by my learned brother in his judgment that it is needless to restate the factual aspect of the case. 

 39. This case being not one of simple case of offer and acceptance and drawing up of a formal written agreement only, the entire fact of the case is to be considered along with surrounding facts and circumstances, the intention of the parties and all other contemporaneous documents for construing what really is the contract in the present case. The proceedings of the 87th meeting of the Planning and Development Committee of the University, few days prior to the work order and the formal contract assume a great importance in the case, wherein between the parties there was negotiations as to the quantum of earth which is to be cut by the appellant and the price was fixed at Tk. 34,00,000.00 for cutting of 32,00,000 cubic feet of earth. Both the appellant and the respondent were present in the said meeting and the intention of the parties was crystal clear from the proceeding of the 87th meeting of the P&D Committee. It may be mentioned that the work order also contains a reference to the proceedings of the two meetings namely, 84th meeting and 87th meeting of the P & D Committee of the University. 

 40. In the background of the case as stated above, the main question that comes up whether the Arbitrator has correctly considered the proceeding of the 87th meeting of the P&D Committee to arrive at a correct interpretation of the contract in the present case. 

 41. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent, submits, that in the formal contract there was no mention of specific quantum of land to be cut from the hill and the contract for item No. 1 being for lump sum amount, the proceeding of the 87th meeting though referred in the work order should not have been considered by the Arbitrator and as such the Arbitrator has mis-conducted himself in arriving at the decision in the case. 

 42. To answer this point, we are to see whether mere non-mentioning as to the quantum of earth in the contract affects the contract in the present case as because a concluded and binding contract had already been established between the parties as evident from the earlier proceedings of the 87th meeting of the P&D Committee. The mere fact that the execution of the formal contract was made at a subsequent point of time is irrelevant as because the parties intended before the formal contract to bind themselves into a binding contract (bargain). The intention of the parties in view of the special circumstances of the case, is so evident that in the facts of the case the contract must be read along with the contemporaneous proceedings of the 87th meeting. In this regard, the case of Kollipara Srira Mulu Vs. T Aswath Narayana reported in AIR 1968 (SC) 2028 may be referred. In that reported decision their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India in view of the special circumstances of the case held that the intention of the parties was of prime consideration and the drawing up of a subsequent written agreement will not affect the validity of a binding and concluded contract reached earlier between the parties. 

 43. In the present case, the parties intended to enter into a contract for cutting of 32,00,000 cubic feet of earth at a price of Tk. 34,00,000.00 and in fact they entered into a binding contract earlier which was not a condition precedent of the drawing up of a formal written contract. Hence, I find it difficult to accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent that the decision of the 87th meeting was ineffective in law because in the formal written contract there was no mention of the quantum of earth to be cut by the contractor. The mere omission to mention the quantum of earth to be cut does not affect the completeness of the contract because the vital terms of the contract with regard to item No.1 of the contract, like the price and the quantum of earth to be cut were all fixed between the parties. I may also refer to the case of Haricharan Mancharan Vs. Govind Luximan Goshall reported in AIR 1923 Privy Council 47, wherein it was held that whether the agreement is a completed bargain or merely a provisional arrangement depends on the intention of the parties as deducible from the language used by the parties on the occasion when the negotiations take a concrete shape. Similar view has also been expressed in the case of Currimbhoy &Co. Ltd. Vs. LA Creet and others reported in AIR 1933 Privy Council 29. Hence, Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed failed to make good his argument on this point. 

 44. I may further point out with reference to the award that the Arbitrator examined witnesses, admitted in evidence a large number of papers and also made a joint survey of the total quantum of earth of the hill and there is no apparent error on the face of the record. The award seems to be a well reasoned award based on the evidence as adduced by the parties. The award is ordinarily final and conclusive between the parties and the court in selling aside the award does not exercise appellate power. We cannot also inquire into the matter as to how the evidence was appreciated by the Arbitrator. Thus, there being no misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator, the learned Judges of the High Court Division wrongly interfered with the award. 

 Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submitted that in an appropriate case the question of the authority of the Arbitrator in granting interest may be considered. At the present I may point out that there are various decisions of the Supreme Court of India on the question of awarding interest by the Arbitrator when a reference is made before the Arbitrator claiming interest. In an appropriate case the authority of the Arbitrator to award interest may be considered. But in the present case interest was set aside by my learned brother by giving good reasons on the fact of this case.
